To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

pulsed microwaves can induce behavioral deficits in rats performing in the radial-arm maze, that the deficits can be reversed by pretreatment with cholinergic or opiate receptor agonists, and that the behavioral deficits are not due to peripheral effects of the microwaves.
microwave irradiation affects radial maze performance in the adult rat and that this effect is reversed by pretreatment with physostigmine, naltrexone and possibly naloxone methioide.
microwave irradiation of the rat brain affects spatial memory performance and that the effect of microwaves can be reversed by pretreatment with physostigmine and naltrexone.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of microwave irradiation on the central nervous system and its behavioral correlates.
the effects of microwave exposure on the cholinergic and opioid systems of the brain, and how these systems may mediate behavioral effects in the rat.
the effects of exposure to microwaves (2450 MHz) in the rat on spatial memory performance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the microwave irradiation affects spatial memory function by a mechanism involving both cholinergic neurotransmission in the brain and activation of the endogenous opioid system.
microwave exposure affects spatial working memory in rats.
microwave irradiation at 2.45 GHz, 1 m W/cm2, 2 microseconds pulses, at 500 pps and 45 min of continuous exposure to the brain, can produce a spatial memory deficit.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

microwave irradiation can induce behavioral deficits in rats performing a spatial learning task in the radial arm-maze, which can be reversed by pretreatment with physostigmine and naloxone methioindide.
microwave irradiation affects the cholinergic and opioid systems in the brain, which in turn affect the spatial working memory.
the effects of microwave irradiation on the brain are not limited to the induction of hyperthermia.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the microwave radiation affects the spatial memory in rats, and that the effect can be reversed by pretreatment with cholinergic and/or opioid agonists.
the microwave exposure induced memory deficit is not a simple effect of hyperthermia.
microwaves are capable of inducing changes in brain function that are not necessarily reflected in changes in body temperature.
